claim: The study analyzed 5534 fecal samples from 56 baboon hosts collected over 13 years (between 2000 and 2013).
source: here we combine extensive time series data on the stool-associated microbiota with a multinomial logistic-normal modeling framework (Figure 1; n=5534 samples from 56 baboons; 75–181 samples per baboon across 6–13.3 years, between 2000 and 2013; Alberts and Altmann, 2012; Björk et al., 2022; Grieneisen et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample size, number of hosts, and time period of data collection with citations to prior work.

claim: Each baboon host in the dataset was sampled at least 75 times with a mean of 99 samples per host.
source: Each baboon host in this data set was sampled at least 75 times (mean number of samples=99; range=75–181 samples; median number of days between samples within hosts=20 days; 25th percentile=7 days, 75th percentile=49 days).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistics about sampling frequency per host.

claim: Most bacterial correlations within individual baboons are weak and negative.
source: We find that, most bacterial correlations are weak, negative, and universal across hosts, such that shared correlation patterns dominate over host-specific correlations by almost twofold.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding about the nature of bacterial correlations.

claim: Shared bacterial correlation patterns dominate over host-specific correlations by almost twofold.
source: We find that, most bacterial correlations are weak, negative, and universal across hosts, such that shared correlation patterns dominate over host-specific correlations by almost twofold.
evidence: The abstract explicitly quantifies the ratio of shared to host-specific correlation patterns.

claim: Taxon pairs with inconsistent correlation signs across hosts always had weak correlations within hosts.
source: Further, taxon pairs that had inconsistent correlation signs (either positive or negative) in different hosts always had weak correlations within hosts.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this relationship between sign consistency and correlation strength.

claim: Host pairs with the most similar bacterial correlation patterns also had similar microbiome taxonomic compositions.
source: From the host perspective, host pairs with the most similar bacterial correlation patterns also had similar microbiome taxonomic compositions and tended to be genetic relatives.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this relationship between correlation patterns and taxonomic composition.

claim: Host pairs with the most similar bacterial correlation patterns tended to be genetic relatives.
source: From the host perspective, host pairs with the most similar bacterial correlation patterns also had similar microbiome taxonomic compositions and tended to be genetic relatives.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this relationship between correlation patterns and genetic relatedness.

claim: Universality in baboons was similar to that in human infants and stronger than in one dataset from human adults.
source: Compared to humans, universality in baboons was similar to that in human infants, and stronger than one data set from human adults.
evidence: The abstract explicitly compares universality across different host populations.

claim: Bacterial families that showed universal correlations in human infants were often universal in baboons.
source: Bacterial families that showed universal correlations in human infants were often universal in baboons.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this cross-species consistency in universal correlations.

claim: Ecological relationships between bacteria mediate the services that gut microbiomes provide to their hosts.
source: Ecological relationships between bacteria mediate the services that gut microbiomes provide to their hosts.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this general principle about bacterial relationships and microbiome function.

claim: Mammalian gut microbiomes exhibit the full spectrum of ecological relationships from mutualism to competition, parasitism, and predation.
source: Mammalian gut microbiomes are highly diverse, dynamic communities whose members exhibit the full spectrum of ecological relationships, from strong mutualisms like syntrophy and cross-feeding, to competition, parasitism, and predation (Faust and Raes, 2012; Foster and Bell, 2012; Dolinšek et al., 2016; Seth and Taga, 2014).
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes the range of ecological relationships with supporting citations.

claim: Microbial relationships mediate metabolism of complex carbohydrates and toxins, and synthesis of short-chain fatty acids, neurotransmitters, and vitamins.
source: These relationships mediate a variety of biological processes that have powerful effects on host health and fitness, including the metabolism of complex carbohydrates and toxins, and the synthesis of physiologically important compounds, like short-chain fatty acids, neurotransmitters, and vitamins (Faust and Raes, 2012; Foster and Bell, 2012; Dolinšek et al., 2016; Seth and Taga, 2014; Bäckhed et al., 2005; Gould et al., 2018; Pontrelli et al., 2022; Degnan et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction explicitly lists these biological processes with supporting citations.

claim: Strong positive bacterial interdependencies can hamper community assembly and stability.
source: Ecological theory predicts that strong positive interactions should be rare in natural communities because species interdependencies can hamper community assembly and stability (Coyte et al., 2015; Coyte et al., 2021).
evidence: The discussion explicitly states this theoretical prediction with supporting citations.

claim: Only 19% of ASV-ASV correlations were stronger than expected by chance (FDR≤0.05).
source: Consistent with the expectation that most bacterial correlations in the gut microbiome are weak (Coyte et al., 2015; Coyte et al., 2021), only 19% of ASV-ASV correlations in the heat map in Figure 2A were stronger than expected by chance (FDR≤0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 3; 19% of phylum-phylum; 22% of family/order/class correlations; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this statistical finding with reference to figures.

claim: Only 3.8% of ASV pairs were significantly positively correlated.
source: In support of the idea that strong, positive bacterial interdependencies are rare (Coyte et al., 2015; Palmer and Foster, 2022; Coyte et al., 2021), only 3.8% of ASV pairs were significantly positively correlated, and the overall bacterial correlation patterns were slightly skewed toward negative relationships.
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this percentage with supporting citations.

claim: At the ASV level, the median correlation coefficient was -0.072, and 60% of correlations were negative.
source: For instance, at the ASV level, the median correlation coefficient in Figure 2A was –0.072, and 60% of these correlations were negative (binomial test p<0.0001).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these statistics with a statistical test.

claim: For family/order/class-level taxa, 58% of all correlations were negative with a median correlation of -0.049.
source: For family/order/class-level taxa, 58% of all correlations were negative (Figure 2—figure supplements 1A and 3A; median family/order/class-level correlation = −0.049; binomial test p<0.0001).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these statistics with references to figures.

claim: 64% of phyla-phyla correlations had a negative sign with a median correlation of -0.100.
source: Correlations between phyla exhibited the strongest negative skew, with 64% of phyla-phyla correlations having a negative sign (Figure 2—figure supplements 1B and 3A; median phyla-level correlation = −0.100; binomial test p<0.0001).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these statistics with references to figures.

claim: No taxon pairs were strongly and inconsistently correlated across hosts.
source: First, in support of the idea that ASVs do not exhibit vastly different correlative relationships in different hosts, no taxon pairs were strongly and inconsistently correlated across hosts (Figure 3A and B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: ASV pairs with inconsistent correlation signs across hosts always had weak and often non-significant median absolute correlation coefficients within hosts.
source: Instead, the ASV pairs that had inconsistent correlation signs across hosts always had weak and often non-significant median absolute correlation coefficients within hosts (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The results section explicitly describes this relationship with reference to figures.

claim: Pairs of ASVs with the most consistent sign agreement across hosts exhibited the largest median absolute correlation coefficients.
source: Second, the pairs with the most consistent sign agreement across hosts also exhibited the largest median absolute correlation coefficients across hosts (Figure 3A and B; Spearman's r=0.844, p<0.0001).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this relationship with a statistical correlation.

claim: For ASV pairs with universal agreement in correlation sign across all hosts, the median absolute correlation coefficient is 0.359.
source: Indeed, for the sets of positively or negatively correlated ASV pairs that showed universal agreement in the sign of their correlation across all hosts (i.e. where x=1 in Figure 3A and B), the median absolute correlation coefficient is 0.359, compared to 0.116 for those with no sign consistency (x=0.5 in Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these specific values with reference to figures.

claim: Population-level signatures contributed between 60% and 80% (median 70%) to observed correlation patterns across hosts.
source: In support of prior observations of 'universality' (Bashan et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2020; Vila et al., 2020; San-Juan-Vergara et al., 2018), we found that, across hosts, the optimal mixture involved contributions from the shared correlation structure (i.e. m) of between 60% and 80% (median 70%) and a host-level contribution (i.e. from e) of between 40% and 20% (median 30%).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these percentages with supporting citations.

claim: The median population:host ratio for correlation patterns was 2.33:1.
source: Hence, population-level signatures contributed almost twice the weight as host-level signatures (a median population:host ratio of 2.33:1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this ratio with reference to a figure.

claim: 48% of universality scores were higher than expected by chance (FDR≤0.05).
source: However, 48% of these scores were higher than expected by chance (permutation test; FDR≤0.05; Figure 3C; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), reflecting a signal of universality in our data.
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this percentage with statistical test information.

claim: In the top 5% most universal ASV pairs, 46 pairs exhibited net positive correlations and 48 pairs exhibited net negative correlations.
source: For instance, in the top 5% most universal ASV pairs (n=94 pairs), 46 pairs exhibited net positive correlations and 48 pairs, net negative correlations, suggesting no particular bias in the direction of the strongest and most consistent associations.
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these counts.

claim: ASV1 (genus Bifidobacterium) was connected to 14 other ASVs in the most universal network.
source: A handful of ASVs were highly connected within this network, especially ASV1 (genus Bifidobacterium; Supplementary file 1a and d), which was connected to 14 other ASVs.
evidence: The results section explicitly identifies this ASV and its connectivity with reference to supplementary files.

claim: Pairings between members of the same family were enriched by >3-fold in the most universal network.
source: Pairings between members of the same family were enriched by >3-fold in this network (p<0.0001), making up 32% of pairs in the most universal set versus only 9.8% of pairs outside that set.
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this enrichment statistic with a p-value.

claim: For positively correlated ASV pairs, closely related taxa had higher universality scores than more distantly related taxa (Pearson's r = -0.232; p<0.0001).
source: In support of the idea that homology leads closely related ASVs to respond similarly to the environment, or perhaps facilitate each other's growth (Meehan and Beiko, 2014; Vacca et al., 2020), we found that, for positively associated ASV pairs, closely related taxa had higher universality scores than more distantly related taxa (Pearson's r for positively correlated pairs = −0.232; p<0.0001; Figure 4A).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this correlation statistic with citations and figure reference.

claim: For negatively correlated ASV pairs, there was a weak positive relationship between phylogenetic distance and universality (Pearson's r=0.106; p=0.004).
source: In contrast, when ASV pairs were negatively correlated, there was a weak positive relationship between phylogenetic distance and universality (Pearson's r=0.106; p=0.004; Figure 4B).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this correlation statistic with figure reference.

claim: 34% of variation in correlation patterns was explained by baseline microbiome community composition (Mantel: r2=0.336; p=0.001).
source: Indeed, a Mantel test correlating compositional distance of average microbial profiles (as Aitchison distances between the per-host mean of CLR-transformed samples) with distance in microbial correlation patterns between hosts revealed that 34% of the variation in correlation patterns was explained by baseline microbiome community composition (Mantel: r2=0.336; p=0.001; Figure 5A; Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this statistical result with figure and supplementary file references.

claim: Host genetic relatedness showed a weak but significant relationship with distance in microbial correlation patterns (r2=0.009; partial Mantel p=0.002).
source: Consistent with prior research in our population, which finds widespread heritability for gut microbiome taxon abundances (Grieneisen et al., 2021), we also found a weak but significant relationship between host genetic distance and the distance in microbial correlation patterns between hosts, after controlling for similarity of baseline composition across hosts. Hosts who were more closely related based on a multigenerational pedigree have slightly more similar ASV-level correlation matrices (Figure 5B; Supplementary file 1g; r2=0.009; partial Mantel controlling for baseline similarity: p-value = 0.002).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this statistical result with citation and figure references.

claim: There was no evidence that members of the same social group exhibit more similar microbial correlation patterns (F=2.146; p=0.089).
source: We found no evidence that members of the same social group or sex exhibit more similar microbial correlation patterns (social group: F=2.146; p=0.089; sex: F=2.026; p=0.160; Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this statistical result with supplementary file reference.

claim: There was no evidence that host sex predicts similarity in microbial correlation patterns (F=2.026; p=0.160).
source: We found no evidence that members of the same social group or sex exhibit more similar microbial correlation patterns (social group: F=2.146; p=0.089; sex: F=2.026; p=0.160; Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this statistical result with supplementary file reference.

claim: There was no evidence that microbial correlations get stronger or weaker with age.
source: We found no evidence that microbial correlations get stronger or weaker with age (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with figure reference.

claim: ASV correlation patterns were slightly more similar within versus between adjacent age classes (juvenile vs. prime age, ANOVA p=0.00175, 1.3% variance explained).
source: Further, ASV correlation patterns were slightly more similar within versus between adjacent age classes (juvenile vs. prime age, ANOVA p=0.00175, 1.3% variance explained; prime age vs. older adult, ANOVA p=0.0112, 0.9% variance explained).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these statistical results.

claim: Removing seasonal trends had little effect on ASV-ASV correlations, with correlation estimates almost identical to the original model (Pearson's r=0.982, p<0.0001).
source: Removing the seasonal trend had little effect on ASV-ASV correlations, as the variance explained by seasonal oscillation was small for all ASVs (median 1.1%, minimum = 0%, maximum = 6%). Consequently, the between-ASV correlation estimates were almost identical to those derived from our original model (Pearson's r=0.982, p<0.0001; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this correlation statistic with figure reference.

claim: ASV pairs with at least one 'seasonal' member had only slightly higher universality scores than pairs where neither partner was seasonal (difference of 0.018; p<0.0001).
source: Further, ASV pairs where one or more members was from a family that showed strong seasonal changes in a prior analysis of these data (Björk et al., 2022), henceforth 'seasonal' families, had only slightly higher universality scores than taxon pairs where neither partner showed strong seasonal changes in abundance (difference of 0.018; p<0.0001; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this statistical result with citation and figure reference.

claim: Estimates of synchrony ranged from 0.033 to 0.474 with a median of 0.187.
source: Estimates of synchrony ranged from 0.033 to 0.474 (median=0.187).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these synchrony statistics.

claim: ASVs in the 13 'seasonal' families are not more likely to have high synchrony than other families (ANOVA, p=0.434).
source: Interestingly, ASVs in the 13 'seasonal' families are not more likely to have high synchrony than other families (ANOVA, p=0.434; Figure 4—figure supplement 4; Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this statistical result with figure and supplementary file references.

claim: The average synchrony of an ASV-ASV pair had a statistically significant but weak relationship with that pair's universality score (r=0.116, p<0.0001).
source: The average synchrony of an ASV-ASV pair had a statistically significant but weak relationship with that pair's universality score (r=0.116, p<0.0001; Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this correlation statistic with figure reference.

claim: Baboons in Amboseli exhibited comparable evidence of universality to the DIABIMMUNE infant/toddler cohort.
source: Contrary to our expectations, we find comparable evidence of universality in baboons and the DIABIMMUNE infant/toddler cohort, but weaker evidence for universality in Johnson et al. (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this comparison with figure reference.

claim: The DIABIMMUNE cohort yielded universality scores slightly higher than those observed in Amboseli (median=0.216 for DIABIMMUNE vs. 0.150 for Amboseli).
source: Bacterial families in the DIABIMMUNE cohort yielded universality scores slightly higher than those observed in Amboseli (25th percentile=0.142, median=0.216, 75th percentile=0.321 for DIABIMMUNE; 25th percentile=0.088, median=0.150, 75th percentile=0.234 for Amboseli), driven by correlations between families that were stronger on average than those estimated for baboons (median DIABIMMUNE family-family correlation strength=0.253; median Amboseli family-family correlation strength=0.170).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these comparative statistics.

claim: Median correlation strengths and universality scores for the Johnson et al., 2019, cohort were substantially lower than the DIABIMMUNE cohort or the baboons.
source: Median correlation strengths and universality scores for the Johnson et al., 2019, cohort were substantially lower (median correlation=0.090; 25th percentile universality=0.050, median=0.086, 75th percentile=0.113) than the DIABIMMUNE cohort or the baboons.
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these comparative statistics with citation.

claim: All of the top 5% most universal family pairs (30 of 30 pairs) are positively associated in the DIABIMMUNE cohort.
source: Further, the most universal family-family associations skewed positive in both the baboons and the infant data set. All of the top 5% most universal family pairs (30 of 30 pairs) are positively associated in the DIABIMMUNE cohort, compared to 70% (23 of 33 pairs) in the Amboseli baboons.
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these counts.

claim: For overlapping family pairs, universality scores in the Amboseli data predicted scores in the DIABIMMUNE data set (r=0.562, p=0.001).
source: For these overlapping pairs, scores in the Amboseli data predicted scores for the same family-family pair in the DIABIMMUNE data set (r=0.562, p=0.001).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this correlation statistic.

claim: The association between universality scores in the Amboseli data and the Johnson et al. data was negative but not statistically significant (r=-0.402, p=0.071).
source: The association between scores in the Amboseli data and the Johnson et al. data was negative, but not statistically significant (r=−0.402, p=0.071).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this correlation statistic with citation.

claim: The baboons were subjects of long-term research by the Amboseli Baboon Research Project in Kenya, which has been studying baboon ecology and behavior since 1971.
source: The baboons were the subject of long-term research on individually recognized animals by the Amboseli Baboon Research Project in Kenya, which has been studying baboon ecology and behavior in the Amboseli ecosystem since 1971 (Alberts and Altmann, 2012).
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes the study population with citation.

claim: The microbiome profiles were derived from PCR amplification of an ~390-bp-long fragment encompassing the V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene using primers 515F-806R.
source: The microbiome compositional profiles are derived from PCR amplification of an ~390-bp-long fragment that encompassed the V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene using primers 515F-806R.
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the sequencing approach.

claim: All samples were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 with a median read count of 48,827 reads per sample.
source: All samples were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2500, with a median read count of 48,827 reads per sample across all 5534 samples (range=982–459,315 reads per sample).
evidence: The methods section explicitly provides sequencing platform and read count statistics.

claim: After filtering, the resulting dataset included 1878 pairs of CLR-transformed ASVs.
source: After filtering, the resulting data set included (1) 1878 pairs of centered log-ratio (CLR)-transformed amplicon sequence variants (ASVs; Figure 2A); (2) 57 pairs of bacterial phyla (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); and (3) 473 pairs of taxa agglomerated to the most granular possible family, order, or class (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides the number of ASV pairs after filtering with figure references.

claim: The filtering steps reduced the number of unique ASVs from 22,097 before filtering to 107 after filtering.
source: At the ASV level, these filtering steps eliminate a majority of ASVs and ASV pairs from consideration: from 22,097 unique ASVs before filtering to 107 after filtering.
evidence: The methods section explicitly provides these counts.

claim: The filtering retained 12 phyla and 35 taxa at the class/order/family level.
source: This filtering also retained 12 phyla and 35 taxa at the class/order/family level (Supplementary file 1a-1c).
evidence: The methods section explicitly provides these counts with supplementary file reference.

claim: The strongest negatively correlated ASV pair included an ASV in family Kiritimatiellae and another in family Lachnospiraceae with a median correlation of -0.520 (±0.132 s.d.).
source: The strongest negatively correlated pair in Figure 2A included an ASV in the family Kiritimatiellae and another in family Lachnospiraceae which had a median correlation of –0.520 (±0.132 s.d.) across all baboon hosts (Figure 2C; ASV19 and ASV23; Supplementary file 1a and d).
evidence: The results section explicitly identifies these ASVs and their correlation with figure and supplementary file references.

claim: The strongest positively correlated ASV pair included two members of genus Prevotella with a median correlation of 0.801 (±0.053 s.d.).
source: The strongest positively correlated pair of ASVs included two members of the genus Prevotella that had a median correlation of 0.801 (±0.053 s.d.) across all baboons (Figure 2D; ASV2 and ASV3; Supplementary file 1a and d).
evidence: The results section explicitly identifies these ASVs and their correlation with figure and supplementary file references.

claim: The two most strongly positively correlated Prevotella ASVs had 97.6% V4 16S DNA sequence identity, indicating they are probably not duplicate 16S gene copies.
source: While these two ASVs were assigned to the same genus, their V4 16S DNA sequence identity was 97.6%, indicating they are probably not simply duplicate 16S gene copies encoded in the genome of a single species (Vetrovský and Baldrian, 2013 Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this sequence identity with citation and supplementary file reference.

claim: Zeros comprised 29.7% of the ASV-level count matrix, 16.1% of the class/order/family count matrix, and 9.8% of the phylum level count matrix.
source: Zeros comprised 29.7% of the ASV-level count matrix, 16.1% of the class/order/family count matrix, and 9.8% of the phylum level count matrix.
evidence: The methods section explicitly provides these percentages of zero values.

claim: High-frequency joint zero abundances for a pair of taxa increased the apparent positive correlation of those taxa.
source: This abundance of 'missing' observations at the ASV level led to a bias in estimates of taxon-taxon correlation: a high-frequency joint zero abundances for a pair of taxa increased the apparent positive correlation of those taxa (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes this bias with figure reference showing the relationship.

claim: The study restricted analyses to taxon pairs with strictly less than 5% frequency of joint absence and less than 50% frequency of absence in either taxon individually.
source: To avoid this bias, we restricted our analyses to taxon pairs with strictly less than a 5% frequency of joint absence (i.e. joint zero abundance observations in less than 5% of all samples across hosts) and less than a 50% frequency of absence in either taxon individually across all samples.
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes these filtering criteria.

claim: After filtering for joint absence, 1878 of the original 7750 ASV-ASV pairs remained in the 'high-confidence' set.
source: After filtering, 1878 of the original 7750 ASV-ASV pairs remained in this 'high-confidence' set.
evidence: The methods section explicitly provides these counts.

claim: At the phylum level, 86.4% (57 of 66 pairs) were included in the high-confidence set.
source: This procedure was also carried out at the phylum and class/order/family levels. However, as the frequency of absence was generally small at these higher taxonomic levels, a higher proportion of possible taxon-taxon pairs were included in the high-confidence set: 86.4% (57 of 66 pairs) at the phylum level and 71.0% (473 of 666 pairs) at the class/order/family level.
evidence: The methods section explicitly provides these percentages and counts.

claim: At the class/order/family level, 71.0% (473 of 666 pairs) were included in the high-confidence set.
source: This procedure was also carried out at the phylum and class/order/family levels. However, as the frequency of absence was generally small at these higher taxonomic levels, a higher proportion of possible taxon-taxon pairs were included in the high-confidence set: 86.4% (57 of 66 pairs) at the phylum level and 71.0% (473 of 666 pairs) at the class/order/family level.
evidence: The methods section explicitly provides these percentages and counts.

claim: The universality score is calculated by multiplying the pair's median absolute correlation coefficient across hosts with its correlation consistency across hosts.
source: The score multiplies the pair's median absolute correlation coefficient across hosts (y-axis of Figure 3A and B) with its correlation consistency across hosts (i.e. proportion of shared sign; x-axis of Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the calculation of the universality score with figure references.

claim: The universality score ranges from 0 to 1, where a score of 1 indicates perfect universality.
source: The resulting scores range from 0 to 1, where a score of 1 equates to perfect 'universality' (i.e. all hosts have a correlation coefficient of 1 or all hosts have a correlation coefficient of –1).
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the range and interpretation of the universality score.

claim: Three other ASVs were connected to at least 10 other ASVs in the most universal network, including members of families Atopobiaceae (ASV8), Eggerthellaceae (ASV28), and Muribaculaceae (ASV86).
source: Three other ASVs were connected to at least 10 other ASVs, including members of families Atopobiaceae (ASV8), Eggerthellaceae (ASV28), and Muribaculaceae (ASV86) (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: The results section explicitly identifies these ASVs and their connectivity with supplementary file reference.

claim: Almost two-thirds of same-family pairs in the most universal set were Prevotellaceae-Prevotellaceae pairs (10 of 16 same-family pairs).
source: Almost two-thirds of these were Prevotellaceae-Prevotellaceae pairs (10 of 16 same-family pairs).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this count and proportion.

claim: The correlation for a given pair of ASVs was only weakly predicted by bacterial abundance (r=0.129 and r=0.223 for the more and less abundant partner respectively; p<0.0001 both).
source: Note, that the correlation for a given pair of ASVs was only weakly predicted by bacterial abundance (r=0.129 and r=0.223 for the more and less abundant partner in a pair respectively; p<0.0001 both).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these correlation statistics.

claim: Bacterial abundance explained only 6% of the variance in median correlation.
source: While this effect was statistically significant, it explained only 6% of the variance in median correlation.
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this variance explained statistic.

claim: The variance explained by seasonal oscillation was small for all ASVs (median 1.1%, minimum = 0%, maximum = 6%).
source: Removing the seasonal trend had little effect on ASV-ASV correlations, as the variance explained by seasonal oscillation was small for all ASVs (median 1.1%, minimum = 0%, maximum = 6%).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these variance statistics.

claim: The trend between correlation strength and sign consistency was strongest in Amboseli baboons (exponent of power regression b=1.72; p<0.0001).
source: This trend was strongest in the Amboseli baboons (exponent of power regression b=1.72; p<0.0001); weaker in the DIABIMMUNE cohort (b=1.51; p<0.0001) and weakest in Johnson et al., 2019 (b=1.19; p<0.0001).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these regression statistics with citation.

claim: 70% (23 of 33 pairs) of the top 5% most universal family pairs are positively associated in Amboseli baboons.
source: All of the top 5% most universal family pairs (30 of 30 pairs) are positively associated in the DIABIMMUNE cohort, compared to 70% (23 of 33 pairs) in the Amboseli baboons.
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this percentage and count.

claim: 29 family pairs overlapped between Amboseli and DIABIMMUNE datasets.
source: Finally, we examined the relationship between universality scores for family pairs that overlapped between Amboseli and DIABIMMUNE (n=29 pairs), and between Amboseli and Johnson et al., 2019 (Figure 6E; n=21 pairs; only 10 family pairs overlapped between all three data sets).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this count with figure reference.

claim: 21 family pairs overlapped between Amboseli and Johnson et al., 2019 datasets.
source: Finally, we examined the relationship between universality scores for family pairs that overlapped between Amboseli and DIABIMMUNE (n=29 pairs), and between Amboseli and Johnson et al., 2019 (Figure 6E; n=21 pairs; only 10 family pairs overlapped between all three data sets).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this count with figure reference and citation.

claim: Only 10 family pairs overlapped between all three datasets (Amboseli, DIABIMMUNE, and Johnson et al.).
source: Finally, we examined the relationship between universality scores for family pairs that overlapped between Amboseli and DIABIMMUNE (n=29 pairs), and between Amboseli and Johnson et al., 2019 (Figure 6E; n=21 pairs; only 10 family pairs overlapped between all three data sets).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides this count with figure reference and citation.

claim: Personalized microbiota do not arise from host-specific microbiome ecologies.
source: This result would suggest that personalized microbiota—their compositions and dynamics—do not arise from host-specific microbiome ecologies (Bashan et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2020; Vila et al., 2020; San-Juan-Vergara et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction presents this as an inference from the expected finding of universality, with supporting citations.

claim: Shared microbiome ecologies would make designing widely applicable microbiome interventions more attainable than personalized microbiome compositions would suggest.
source: For instance, shared ecologies would mean that designing widely applicable microbiome interventions is a more attainable goal than personalized microbiome compositions would suggest.
evidence: The discussion presents this as a logical implication of the findings.

claim: The correlation patterns observed likely arise from a combination of ecological interactions between bacteria and shared responses to the environment.
source: While mutualisms and universal dynamics are important, the correlation patterns we observe likely arise from a combination of ecological interactions between bacteria and shared responses to the environment (i.e. pairs of bacteria that prefer the same or different environments).
evidence: The discussion explicitly states this interpretation of the findings.

claim: The observed correlations cannot be mapped directly to standard categories of pairwise ecological interactions such as mutualism, commensalism, amensalism, exploitation, or competition.
source: We note that none of the correlations we observed can be mapped directly to standard categories of pairwise ecological interactions, such as mutualism, commensalism, amensalism, exploitation, or competition.
evidence: The discussion explicitly states this limitation of the correlational approach.

claim: Experimental approaches that directly measure the effects of one species on another's growth in vitro are better suited to characterizing ecological interactions.
source: Experimental approaches that directly measure the effects of one species on another's growth in vitro are better suited to characterizing these relationships (Kehe et al., 2021; Weiss et al., 2022; Ortiz et al., 2021; Carlström et al., 2019; Venturelli et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion explicitly recommends this approach with supporting citations.

claim: The lack of universality in Johnson et al., 2019 may be due to the difference in sampling time scale (daily vs. monthly).
source: The lack of universality in Johnson et al., 2019, may be due to this difference in sampling time scale, especially if daily abundances and correlations are noisier than covariances modeled over the longer time scales in our study.
evidence: The discussion explicitly proposes this explanation with citation.

claim: The subjects in Johnson et al., 2019 consumed substantially different diets from each other, which may reduce the universality of microbial correlations.
source: The subjects in Johnson et al., 2019, also consumed substantially different diets from each other, perhaps more so than the children in the DIABIMMUNE cohort, and this inter-host difference in diet may reduce the universality of microbial correlations.
evidence: The discussion explicitly proposes this alternative explanation with citation.

claim: ASV-level correlation patterns are expected to be less individualized than strain-level patterns due to functional redundancy within ASVs.
source: Because ASVs encompass multiple species and strains, each with somewhat different functional capacities, their dynamics may be buffered against idiosyncrasies driven by horizontal gene transfer and functional redundancy, which affect single strains more strongly than whole species or genera. We would strain-level correlation patterns to be more individualized than those between ASVs.
evidence: The discussion explicitly proposes this expectation based on taxonomic resolution.

claim: Personalized gut microbial compositions may emerge from personalized assembly processes and interactions driven by rare, host-specific strains.
source: Third, personalized gut microbial compositions may emerge from at least two other phenomena: personalized assembly processes and interactions driven by rare, host-specific strains (which were necessarily excluded from our analyses) (Costello et al., 2012; Walter and Ley, 2011).
evidence: The discussion explicitly proposes these alternative explanations with supporting citations.

claim: Some bacterial families may exhibit consistent microbial relationships within hosts, across host populations, and across host species.
source: Hence, some bacterial families may exhibit consistent microbial relationships within hosts, across host populations, and across host species.
evidence: The discussion explicitly states this conclusion based on the cross-species comparison.

claim: The conserved associations identified may indicate strong partner fidelity or obligate partnerships.
source: While this study lacked resolution at the level of individual hosts, it did identify a conserved network of positively associated and closely related microbes similar to those we identify in Figure 3. The authors speculate that these conserved associations may indicate strong partner fidelity or obligate partnerships.
evidence: The discussion cites speculation from another study about the meaning of conserved associations.

claim: The baboons range over the same habitat and experience similar diets and sources of microbial colonization.
source: The baboons range over the same habitat and experience similar diets and sources of microbial colonization, facilitating inference about the consistency of microbial correlations across hosts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Björk et al., 2022; Grieneisen et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes the environmental similarity of the study population with citations and figure reference.

claim: The modeling approach controls for variation attributable to seasonal changes in the animals' diets, proportionality in the count data, and irregularity in sampling.
source: To partly account for environmental drivers of microbial dynamics, our modeling approach controls for variation attributable to seasonal changes in the animals' diets, proportionality in the count data, and irregularity in sampling to produce per-individual, per-taxon trajectories of log-ratio abundances that we used to estimate pairwise microbial correlations within each host.
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes what the modeling approach controls for.

claim: Each baboon exhibits a somewhat distinctive gut microbial community (p<0.0001; ANOVA).
source: Each baboon exhibits a somewhat distinctive gut microbial community (p<0.0001; ANOVA) summarized here by the first two principal components of centered log-ratio (CLR)-transformed amplicon sequence variant (ASV) abundances of ASVs during six representative years of sample collection (see Figure 1B).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2 caption explicitly states this finding with statistical test and figure reference.

claim: The DIABIMMUNE cohort consists of 285 samples collected monthly over 3 years from 15 infants and toddlers living in Russian Karelia.
source: and the DIABIMMUNE cohort that consists of 285 samples, collected monthly over 3 years, from 15 infants and toddlers living in Russian Karelia (Vatanen et al., 2016; at the time of writing, these cohorts were the only publicly available data sets we could find that included large numbers of repeated samples from the same subjects).
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes this human dataset with citation.

claim: The Johnson et al. dataset includes daily samples from 34 human adults over a 17-day span (483 total samples).
source: daily samples from 34 human adults over a 17-day span (483 total samples; hereafter Johnson et al., 2019)
evidence: The introduction explicitly describes this human dataset with citation.

claim: At the time of writing, the DIABIMMUNE and Johnson et al. cohorts were the only publicly available datasets with large numbers of repeated samples from the same subjects.
source: and the DIABIMMUNE cohort that consists of 285 samples, collected monthly over 3 years, from 15 infants and toddlers living in Russian Karelia (Vatanen et al., 2016; at the time of writing, these cohorts were the only publicly available data sets we could find that included large numbers of repeated samples from the same subjects).
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this limitation in available datasets with citation.

claim: Family/order/class taxonomic levels offered the greatest comparative power between datasets (10.1% overlap) compared to genera (3.1% overlap) and ASVs (no overlap).
source: Here, we compared each host cohort's universality at the level of correlations between families, orders, and classes because these taxonomic levels offered the greatest comparative power (10.1% of families/orders/classes overlap between the cohorts compared to just 3.1% of genera and no ASVs).
evidence: The results section explicitly provides these overlap percentages to justify the taxonomic level chosen.
